newsitem.title: USA: Ohio school funding overhaul stalls in legislature.
newsitem.headline: Ohio school funding overhaul stalls in legislature.

text.p: Ohio lawmakers late Sunday failed to reach an accord on overhauling the state's public school financing system, making it unlikely the issue will be put before voters in November, a legislative aide said.

Lawmakers are not expected to meet a Wednesday deadline to place proposed tax increases and expanded bond authority on the ballot, said Elizabeth Coleman, an aide to House Speaker Jo Anne Davidson, R-Reynoldsburg.
Representatives late Sunday rejected a sales tax increase approved last week by the Senate to generate $1.1 billion annually for public schools.

Senators refused to concur with the substitution shortly thereafter, leaving the issue unresolved as Ohio legislators gathered Monday morning for services for former House Speaker Vern Riffe, who died last week.

Ohio Supreme Court justices in March overturned the state's education funding method, which they found relied too heavily on local property taxes. The justices gave lawmakers one year to adopt a new method.

A task force named by Gov. George Voinovich recommended raising the state sales tax to provide $1.1 billion of revenues annually to reduce dependence on property taxes. The task force also recommended $5.8 billion of bonds for school construction over 10 years.

The Senate plan included the sales tax increase, a property tax increase on businesses and a property tax cut for individuals making the net increase less than the $1.1 billion the task force recommended.
The House proposal earmarked a percentage of the general revenue fund for education and pledged $300 million of bonds per year over 10 years for capital improvements.
Lawmakers approved plans requiring greater fiscal and academic accountability last week by simple majority votes. The proposed tax increases required 60 percent approval for placement on the ballot.
The accountability plan included requiring school districts to create "rainy day" funds and budget forecasts five years into the future.
Under Ohio law, referendum questions must be approved by Wednesday for placement on the November ballot. Legislators could increase taxes without voter approval as well.
